name: Tara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior solicitor at Hale & Okafor, a four-lawyer firm above a bakery on Mill Street, and almost all our work is housing: tenants facing eviction, mould and damp claims, landlords who won't fix the boiler. Most of it is paid by legal aid, which means the government pays us a fixed fee that hasn't really gone up in years. A normal day is phone calls from frightened tenants in the morning, drafting letters to landlords after lunch, and then Ruth, my supervisor, reading my drafts and putting red pen all over them. On Tuesdays I sit at the duty desk in the county court and help whoever walks in with a possession hearing that day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the duty desk best, honestly. Someone comes in shaking with a court letter, and twenty minutes later the judge has adjourned the case and they get to keep their flat for now. What wears me out is the money and the paperwork. I earn less than my friends who went into big firms, I rent a room in a shared house with my friend Dani, who's a care worker, and I have about three weeks of money in the bank. And I'm slow at drafting; Ruth says I'll get there, but I can see her rewriting my letters at nine at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, I told you so. Everyone at my law school reunion was going on about how AI would replace lawyers, and I'd be the one saying the real problem in housing law was never the technology, it was the funding. Online I'd probably share something from the legal aid lawyers' group about fee rates, because that's still the fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze as now, which isn't nothing. The firm lost the second legal aid housing contract last spring, and Ruth said in a meeting that if the fees don't move, she can't promise to keep a junior past next autumn. So AI being hype doesn't save my job; it just means the thing that might end it is a spreadsheet at the legal aid agency, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get faster at drafting, using Ruth's old letters as templates like I do now. I'd join the housing lawyers' network properly and go to their meetings about the fee freeze instead of just reading the emails. And I'd cut the bits I can, like the gym I barely use, so I'm not living on three weeks of savings forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved on one level, because I don't want to learn some chatbot. But mostly the same knot in my stomach I have every month when the rent goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger is a spreadsheet, not a robot. What would you do if Ruth told you next autumn that she can't keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are only two other firms in town that do housing work, and neither is hiring, so I'd be looking at moving to a city or going back to live with my mum. I'd probably try the council's housing advice team first, because at least I'd still be helping tenants. But I'd be earning even less, and I'd be starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym goes first, then the train fare to see my friends on weekends. I already make packed lunches. After that it's the stuff I can't really cut, like my phone, and the professional practising fee, which I need to keep being a solicitor at all.

say: I'd tell people the real threat to **housing law** was always the **funding**, not the technology.
I'd share the **legal aid** lawyers' posts about the **fee freeze**, because that's still the fight.
think: My job is still at risk because the firm **lost a contract** and fees haven't moved.
Ruth can't promise to keep a **junior past autumn**, so hype or not, I'm exposed.
The thing that could end my job is a **legal aid spreadsheet**, not a robot.
do: Get faster at drafting by reusing **Ruth's old letters** as templates.
Join the **housing lawyers' network** meetings on the fee freeze.
Cancel the **gym membership** so I'm not stuck on three weeks of savings.
feel: **Relieved** not to have to learn a chatbot.
Still a **knot in my stomach** every month when rent goes out.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't save my job; it just means the thing that might end it is a spreadsheet at the legal aid agency, not a robot.
fieldNote: Her worry here **isn't AI at all**; it's the firm's lost legal aid contract and the frozen fees.
With **three weeks of savings** and only two other housing firms in town, she has little room.
She's clearly relieved she won't have to **learn new tools**, which fits her dislike of technology.
Her fallback is the **council housing advice** team, lower pay but still helping tenants.

steps.text: Reuse Ruth's old letters as templates to draft faster
Go to the housing lawyers' network meetings on the fee freeze
Cancel the gym and stop weekend train trips if money tightens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like before, I'll read the card first. This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the network meetings: if software is writing the letters, the legal aid agency will use it as an excuse to cut fees again. I'd say tenants still need a human in that court corridor. I'd be the one at the pub saying this is a gift to landlords, who can afford the good tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bit of my job that's writing and checking is the bit I'm worst at, and that's exactly the bit this card says goes first. If a program drafts a disrepair letter in ten seconds, Ruth doesn't need a slow junior to do it in two hours. So I think a firm like ours just doesn't renew a junior, and I'm the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth to put me on the duty desk more days and on client meetings, the parts where you have to be in the room. I'd push the network to campaign for rules that legal aid work needs a qualified person to sign off, not just a program. And I'd start saving every spare bit, maybe fifty a month, because I'd know the end of my contract was coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest, and a bit angry. I trained for six years to do this, and it feels like the ladder is being pulled up just as I got on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from the tools. If Ruth asked you to use the drafting software, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if she told me to, because I can't afford to say no. But I'd check every line, because I've seen what happens when a letter cites the wrong section and the landlord's lawyer laughs at you. I don't trust it, and I'd be slow with it too, which is the joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious, our caseworker, who isn't a lawyer but does all the benefit forms and the housing applications. That's checking and form-filling, which is the first thing on that card. She's got two kids and she's been there eleven years.

say: I'd warn that the **legal aid agency** would use the software to **cut fees** again.
I'd say tenants still need a **human in the corridor** at court.
I'd call it a **gift to landlords**, who can afford the better tools.
think: The **writing and checking** I'm weakest at is exactly what goes first.
A small firm simply **won't renew a junior**, and I'm the junior.
do: Ask Ruth for more **duty desk** days and in-person client meetings.
Push the network to campaign for **qualified sign-off** on legal aid work.
Save about **fifty a month** before my contract runs out.
feel: **Scared** and a bit **angry** about the ladder being pulled up.
S1.quote: I trained for six years to do this, and it feels like the ladder is being pulled up just as I got on it.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **drafting and checking** are both her weak spot and the first thing automated.
Her plan is to **retreat to in-person work**: the court duty desk and client meetings.
She'd use AI only **under orders**, slowly and distrustfully, which she knows makes her weaker.
Her concern for **Precious, the caseworker**, shows she thinks of the whole small team.

steps.text: Ask Ruth for two duty desk days a week instead of one
Push the network to demand qualified sign-off on legal aid work
Put fifty a month aside before the contract ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd just post something furious about how nobody voted for this. At work I'd probably say we need to keep going for the clients who are in court this week, because they still are. People still get evicted on a Tuesday whatever happens in Silicon Valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done as a lawyer within two years. I'm a junior who's below average at the thinking part, and the card says the thinking part is gone by 2028. Robots coming three years later doesn't help me, because my job isn't hands-on; the only physical bit is standing up in court, and I don't know if courts will still want a person standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't have a plan, and that's the scary bit. I'd probably move back into my mum's flat to stop paying rent, which would save me about six hundred a month. I'd vote for whoever promised a basic income or protected jobs, and I'd go to the protests, because I can't think of anything else that would work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest gets tight just thinking about it, and I'm not someone who panics easily in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know if courts will want a person standing there. What would make you hopeful about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the judges and the law society dig in and say a human must represent a human, maybe there's a few of us left doing advocacy. But I'm a junior with one day a week of court experience, so even then I'd be at the back of the queue. The senior barristers would get those jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum when you turned up with your boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not my fault, which is true, but it would still feel like failing. She cleaned offices for twenty years to help pay for my degree. She'd say don't worry, beta, but she'd be worried, and she'd tell all my aunties.

say: I'd post that **nobody voted** for this kind of change.
At work I'd say tenants still get **evicted on a Tuesday**, so we keep going for now.
think: As a **below-average junior**, I think I'm done as a lawyer within **two years**.
Robots coming later doesn't help, because my work is **thinking, not hands-on**.
Even court advocacy would go to **senior barristers** before me.
do: Move back into **mum's flat** to save about **six hundred a month**.
Vote for whoever promises **basic income** or protected jobs.
Go to **protests**, since I can't see another option.
feel: **Panicky**, with a tight chest, even though court doesn't usually rattle me.
S2.quote: Mum cleaned offices for twenty years to help pay for my law degree, and I'd be turning up at her flat with my boxes, saying it's not my fault.
fieldNote: She says outright she has **no plan**, and her only moves are retreat and protest.
She understands the **three-year robot gap** gives a desk-based lawyer nothing.
The **shame of moving home** to her mother, who paid for her degree, hit harder than the job loss.
Her one thread of hope is **courts requiring a human**, but she knows she's at the back.

steps.text: Move back into her mother's flat to save six hundred a month
Lean on her mother for food and rent while she looks
Vote and protest for a basic income or protected jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them. At the network I'd be pushing for the government to fund legal aid properly with a person on every case, before the firms start replacing juniors. Online I'd be less furious and more organised, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd probably get to finish my training contract time and qualify fully, maybe get a few years of court experience. But I think I'd watch the writing work disappear bit by bit from about 2029, and I'd still be the slow one. The robots coming in 2034 don't matter to me; for a lawyer, the date that counts is 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try to move into a job where being there in person is the point, like the council's tenancy relations team, which goes and talks to landlords face to face. I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a month, by taking the cheaper room Dani's cousin has. And I'd stay in the network, because if anyone's going to win a rule about human lawyers, it's a group, not me alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less sick than the two-year one. Five years is enough time to be scared properly, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years is enough time to be scared properly. What does that look like on an ordinary Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like me checking job sites on my lunch break instead of eating with Precious. It looks like reading every news story about legal software and feeling my stomach drop. I'd be doing my job but with one eye on the door the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council job and not learning the tools, like some of your classmates might?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at the tools and they'd still replace me, just a year later. The council job means knocking on a landlord's door and saying fix the damp or we take you to court. A program can write that letter, but I'm not sure it can stand on the doorstep.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get the rules right and shouldn't waste them.
I'd push for **funded legal aid** with a person on every case.
think: Five years probably lets me **qualify fully** and get some court experience.
Writing work would **disappear bit by bit**, and I'd still be the slow one.
For a lawyer the date that counts is **2031**, not the robots in **2034**.
do: Apply to the council's **tenancy relations** team, where face-to-face work is the point.
Take the **cheaper room** and save about **a hundred a month**.
Stay in the **network** to fight for a rule on human lawyers.
feel: **Worried**, but less sick than with two years.
Scared in a **slow, steady** way, every day.
S3.quote: A program can write the letter telling a landlord to fix the damp, but I'm not sure a program can stand on the doorstep.
fieldNote: She sees the **robot delay as irrelevant** to her; her exposure date is the AGI date itself.
Rather than learn AI, she'd **move sideways** into face-to-face council work.
She still expects to **lose her legal role**, which keeps her at alarmed despite the extra time.
The image of **job sites at lunch** shows how the worry would colour every day.

steps.text: Apply to the council's tenancy relations team within the year
Move into the cheaper room and save a hundred a month
Keep campaigning with the network for human lawyers on legal aid cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real window, so the profession has no excuse not to plan. I'd be saying it at the network, at my old law school, anywhere: make the government put rules in place now. And I'd tell the younger students to think hard before they take on the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is almost a whole career stage. I'd be 37 when it arrives, probably fully trained and good at court work by then, and court is the bit I love. I still think the thinking side goes, but a decade is long enough for me to become the person who stands up in court, not the one who types the letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the extra advocacy qualification that lets solicitors argue in the higher courts, even though it costs about two thousand and I'd have to pay it off monthly. I'd build my savings slowly to two months, maybe by picking up weekend shifts at the law centre. And I'd keep doing the duty desk every week, because that's the experience that would matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not calm. I'd still have a little voice at the back saying the courts might not need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the courts might not need you either. What happens at 37 if that voice is right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have ten years of knowing people in this town, and I'd probably end up at the council or an advice charity, working with tenants in person. I wouldn't be rich, but I'd know how to help someone with a court letter. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change in your personal life with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take on a mortgage I couldn't drop if the job went. Dani and I have talked about getting a flat together; I'd still do it, but I'd want a short tenancy, which is funny for a housing lawyer to say.

say: I'd say a **ten-year window** leaves the profession **no excuse** not to plan.
I'd warn law students to think hard before taking on **the debt**.
think: At **37**, I'd likely be fully trained and good at the **court work** I love.
The **thinking side** still goes, but ten years lets me move to advocacy.
do: Take the **higher courts advocacy** course, about **two thousand**, paid monthly.
Pick up **weekend law centre** shifts to build **two months** of savings.
Keep doing the **duty desk** every week for the experience.
feel: **Calmer** than the other pictures, but not calm.
A small **nagging fear** that courts won't need me either.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to become the person who stands up in court, not the one who types the letters.
fieldNote: The decade gives her a **real route**: specialise in **court advocacy**, her strongest skill.
She still expects the **drafting side** of her job to go, so she stays anxious, not calm.
Even this resistant lawyer **plans ahead** once the timeline is long enough.
Her joke about wanting a **short tenancy** shows how the worry reaches her home life.

steps.text: Take the higher courts advocacy course, paying two thousand monthly
Work weekend shifts at the law centre to reach two months' savings
Keep doing the Tuesday duty desk at the county court

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time, no money and no plan. What would help is a rule that anyone facing eviction gets a real person to represent them, paid for properly, so there's still work for people like me. And some kind of income support while people retrain, not just a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. If AI writes all the letters, the people with money get the best lawyers and the people I help get a chatbot. I chose housing law because it's the bit where people really need someone on their side, and a chatbot can't sit next to you in a court corridor while you cry.

headlineQuote: A chatbot can't sit next to you in a court corridor while you cry.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old junior** housing solicitor at a four-lawyer legal aid firm on **Mill Street**.
She has about **three weeks of savings**, rents a room with Dani and earns less than her classmates.
She **distrusts AI tools**, is slow at drafting, and loves the in-person **court duty desk**.
She blames **funding cuts and tech firms**, and turns to the lawyers' network and protest for answers.
Her mood moves from **anxious to panicked** as the timeline shortens, easing only with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have **no time**, no money and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that anyone facing eviction gets a **real person**, properly **funded** by legal aid.
**Income support** while people retrain, not just a leaflet.
